summary.text: Bioluminescence is light produced by a living thing through a chemical reaction.
Usually an enzyme called luciferase oxidizes a substance called luciferin, and the excited product gives off visible light as it settles down.
Animals use the glow for camouflage, to lure prey and to signal mates, and the ability has evolved independently at least 94 times.

facts.label: Earliest glow
facts.value: In octocorals, some 540 million years ago

facts.label: Borrowed light
facts.value: Some animals glow via symbiotic Vibrio bacteria

items.prompt: Why did the US Navy take an interest in glowing sea life during the Cold War?

options.label: It hoped to light ships without fuel
Glowing plankton could jam radar
Submarine wakes can glow and be seen
It wanted to signal divers at night

items.explain: In some waters a submarine leaves a wake bright enough to be detected, so the Navy wanted to predict when that would happen.

items.prompt: Comparing many glowing species, which part of the light-making chemistry differs most from one species to the next?

options.label: The enzyme, luciferase
The substrate, luciferin
The oxygen being used
The type of light emitted

items.explain: Luciferins vary little across evolution, while luciferases vary widely between species.

items.prompt: As a Navy pilot, Jim Lovell lost his navigation systems at night over the ocean. How did he find his aircraft carrier?

options.label: He steered by the stars overhead
He homed in on its radio signal
He spotted the lights on its deck
He followed the ship's glowing wake

items.explain: With his cabin lights off he could see the ship's glowing wake, and he flew to it and landed safely.

items.prompt: An old idea held that glowing animals got their light from phosphorus. What did Raphaël Dubois show instead?

options.label: Phosphorus causes it, but only at night
An enzyme oxidizing a compound causes it
Moonlight reflecting off scales causes it
Static electricity in the air causes it

items.explain: Dubois disproved the phosphorus idea and showed the glow comes from an enzyme oxidizing a compound he named luciferin.

items.prompt: Following Robert Boyle's experiments, you seal a glowworm in a jar and remove all the air. What happens to its light?

options.label: It glows more brightly than before
It shifts to a different colour
It keeps glowing just as before
It stops producing light

items.explain: Boyle showed that glowworms and other glowing sources need air to produce light.

items.prompt: Among animals, where is bioluminescence most widespread?

options.label: In deserts
In caves
In the sea
In forests

items.explain: Bioluminescence is spread across many animal groups, especially in marine environments.

paragraphs.heading: Living light
paragraphs.text: Bioluminescence is light that a living thing makes through a chemical reaction. It shows up in many kinds of life: sea animals with and without backbones, fireflies and other land arthropods, some fungi, and tiny organisms such as certain bacteria and dinoflagellates. It is spread widely across animal groups and is especially common in the sea. On land it is found in fungi, bacteria and some invertebrates, including insects.

paragraphs.heading: How the glow is made
paragraphs.text: In most cases two ingredients do the work: a substance called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. These are general names, so scientists label each by the creature or group it comes from, such as firefly luciferin. In every case studied, the enzyme oxidizes the luciferin, producing an energized molecule called oxyluciferin. As that molecule drops back to its resting state, it releases visible light. Some luciferases also need helpers such as calcium or magnesium ions, and sometimes ATP, a molecule that carries energy.

paragraphs.heading: Invented again and again
paragraphs.text: Some animals make their own light, which is called autogenic. In others the light is bacteriogenic: it comes from partner bacteria living with them, such as members of the genus Vibrio. The ability has evolved separately at least 94 times, starting in octocorals around 540 million years ago. Luciferins change little over evolution; one of them, coelenterazine, appears in 11 animal phyla, and some of those animals get it from their food. Luciferases, by contrast, differ a great deal from one species to another.

paragraphs.heading: What the light is for
paragraphs.text: Animals put their light to several uses. Some use it for a kind of camouflage called counterillumination. Others imitate other animals, for example to lure prey, and some signal to members of their own species, for instance to attract a mate. People have found a use for it too: in laboratories, systems built on luciferase help with genetic engineering and medical research.

paragraphs.heading: Early puzzles
paragraphs.text: People noticed natural glows long before they understood them. Aristotle and Pliny the Elder both wrote that damp wood sometimes shines. Many centuries later Robert Boyle showed that oxygen played a part, in wood, fish and glowworms alike. Proper study only began in the late nineteenth century, when the French pharmacologist Raphaël Dubois showed that the glow did not come from phosphorus but from an enzyme oxidizing a particular compound, which he named luciferin.

paragraphs.heading: A glowing wake
paragraphs.text: A glowing sea can give things away. In some waters a submarine leaves a wake bright enough to be spotted, and during the First World War a German submarine was found this way and sunk. During the Cold War the United States Navy wanted to predict when this could happen, so it could steer its own submarines out of sight. The same glow once helped Jim Lovell, later an Apollo 13 astronaut. As a Navy pilot whose navigation systems had failed, he switched off his cabin lights, saw the shining wake of his aircraft carrier, and followed it back to land safely.
